concept.name: Hot-hand fallacy
concept.definition: The belief that a person or process enjoying a run of successes has an elevated probability of continued success - the 'hot hand'. Gilovich, Tversky and Vallone (1985) found basketball shooting streaks consistent with chance, but Miller and Sanjurjo later showed the original statistical test was itself biased, so the existence of genuine streaks remains contested.
concept.intuition: After three winning trades in a row a trader feels in the zone and sizes up - as if success itself were contagious.
concept.mechanics: It is positive recency: expecting a streak to continue. GTV found shot outcomes statistically independent; Miller and Sanjurjo (2018) showed that in finite sequences the measured hit rate after streaks is biased downward, so equal rates can actually indicate a real hot hand. In trading the fallacy is attributing a winning streak to skill or a hot state without statistical evidence.
concept.failure_modes: The fallacy label can itself be wrong: genuine streaks exist in some domains, and small samples make streak detection statistically fragile. Belief in a hot hand can also become self-reinforcing through confidence and increased risk-taking.
concept.misconceptions: The 1985 study did not prove streaks never exist - it showed observed patterns were consistent with randomness, and its method was later shown to be biased against finding streaks. Winning streaks in trading are nonetheless mostly consistent with luck plus variance.
concept.example: A day trader doubles his size after four straight winning days, believing he is hot; his win rate over the next hundred trades regresses to his long-run average.

citations.section: 1985 'Hot Hand in Basketball' paper; Miller-Sanjurjo reanalysis
